narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated a 59% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than not. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty; it still leaves a meaningful chance of passing, but it crossed the threshold used for this decision. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, far below the average accepted student around the sixth decile. That low standing pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.60, which is above the accepted-student average of 3.23 and therefore pushed toward passing; it helped, but not enough to offset the academic concerns. The third strongest factor was your LSAT score of 26, well below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it also pushed toward failure. To improve your position, meet with admissions to ask whether reconsideration is possible and what evidence would strengthen your file. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, document any upward academic trend or relevant work experience, and seek advising on bar-readiness supports. You may also apply to programs that review applicants holistically.
